en: No example of this has ever been seen within the belly of the three worlds; yet, if one were to imagine even a touch from the True Guru who bestows knowledge, it would surely transform base iron into gold.
Nevertheless, when the True Guru places his own likeness upon a disciple by resting his two feet upon them, that disciple becomes peerless, beyond comparison, and even transcendentally extraordinary.

Just as other trees, by means of the fragrance spreading from a sandalwood tree, constantly partake of its sweet scent and likewise uproot the fever of embodied beings, so too do those whose hearts are compassionate wash away the threefold suffering and sin of those standing near them—though they have themselves received awakening from a teacher—by means of their own words, through the power of destiny. || 2 ||

The cognition of self and non-self was first declared; then, through its connection with truth and falsity, the cognition of Brahman was described as twofold by means of personal experience and logical reasoning. The former arises from attachment to the body, while the latter arises from the state of being the Self of all. First, when the realization "I am Brahman" has dawned, then indeed this world is seen as Brahman. (3)

The Self is indeed the controller of all bodies and the like, familiar through the experience of its own nature as consciousness, awareness, and bliss; yet, alas, even after repeatedly perceiving that one’s own body and those of others are externally filled with bones, sinews, marrow, flesh, blood, fat, skin, fat-tissue, excrement, urine, and phlegm, people of deluded intellect still harbor the notion that the impermanent body is the Self.
"The body, wife, sons, friends, followers, horses, and bulls—these are the causes of my satisfaction; thus they all spend their own lives. Enough with this extensive investigation of flesh here!
Those who are clever in worldly affairs and possess good fortune live by means of that immortal Lord of Life dwelling within them, yet they do not investigate Him at all. (5)
Just as a certain insect of sharp wit, having somehow constructed a hut amidst thorns, exerts itself for its entire life to carry on its activities together with that very structure;
even so, the individual soul (jīva), having fashioned a gross body through actions accumulated by various modes of conduct, remains right here and day after day descends upon the earth along with it.
Does a tiger, assuming the guise of a tiger for the sake of filling its own belly, terrify the simple-minded and thus afflict those animal-like men who think, "I am a tiger"?

Does an actor, wearing a woman's dress, act out the thought, "I am a woman," merely to fulfill his master's wish? In the same way, the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), which experiences itself as distinct from the body, is the Witness (sākṣī).
Just as a mother, in order to quickly bring peace to her own child who has been weeping for a very long time, employs grapes, dates, mangoes, or fine plantains before him;

likewise, the Upaniṣad has thoroughly awakened that extremely deluded mind—which, due to the accumulation of the impressions of ignorance from many births of worldly existence—is otherwise helpless—by means of numerous methods of realization.

That for whose sake one feels affection—whether it be a wife, a youth, a son, wealth, or other such primary objects—is therefore dearer than those things; yet the Self is even more so, while everything else is merely a locus of sorrow. Thus, how could anything else be truly dear? One who desires his own welfare gives away his wife and the like, and even his very body, when seeking the highest good for himself. Therefore, the wise person should worship the Self alone as the supreme object of love, and nothing else.

For as long as there is pleasure here from an object, so long does it possess the quality of being dear; and since suffering certainly arises from it, to that same extent it possesses the quality of being undear. Both [states] do not exist in a single thing at all times; even that which is undear may become dear, or that which is dear may constantly become undear. Therefore, the reality called the Self is eternally dear.

In this world, two kinds of goals are said to exist: the beneficial (*śreyas*) and the pleasant (*preyas*), the latter being sought after for its desires. The pleasant is the sole seed of suffering and becomes bitter in a mere moment; the dull-witted desire it. Brahman alone is the ultimate goal, the abode of unsurpassed bliss; those who know reality take refuge in it. This is declared in the *Kaṭhopaniṣad*, specifically in the sixth chapter (*vallī*).

While walking, he contemplates, "I am a wave of the ocean of the Self"; while seated, he thinks, "I am the jewel threaded upon the string of consciousness," or "I am the perceiver of the objects of the senses";

while lying down, he reflects, "I have been seen through the vision of the Self. That seeker of liberation who, established in the inner state, remains immersed in the ocean of bliss and thus passes his life as a living being—he indeed is the true embodied one.

This entire world, consisting of name and form, is the manifestation of the Vairāja [Self] as the individual; it moves from the Prāṇa which resides within as its primary essence, and through that, one perceives all objects.

He who is full of knowledge and realization understands directly that "this [Self] is neither the doer nor the enjoyer, like the sun"; knowing thus, he acts daily preceded by the contemplation of the Supreme Self.

O Jñānagarbha, renunciation (*nairvedya*) is said to be of two kinds; therein, the first is dispassion (*vairāgya*), which generally arises from observing suffering caused by the desire for home, friends, children, and wealth.

The other arises from the instruction of knowledge, whereby objects that have appeared are regarded as things to be rejected like vomit. Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is also twofold: that of one whose mind is restrained, whether from the body or from the household. (14)

Whatever person in the three worlds strives for the sake of happiness and never for the sake of suffering, there are two causes of that [suffering]: the body, from which [suffering] arises, and the attachment to one's own objects; for one who possesses the constant notion of "self" in the body experiences the affliction of diseases and the like, and when wife, sons, or wealth are lost, he meets with supreme calamity, yet not so when an enemy is destroyed. (15)

Even while remaining at home, the master of the house, like a guest desiring to go to his own abode, no longer experiences the pleasure or pain residing in the body, as he has abandoned the sense of "mine-ness" and egoism. Knowing that this body will come like a mass of clouds and must inevitably depart, he who understands the true nature of things remains free from effort.

Like a snake casting off its skin from itself, he who goes forth from his own home; like a traveler seeking a little shade arising from a tree by the road, he should take refuge in that which resides in the body;

and like one asking for alms-food consisting of fallen fruits from trees sufficient only for hunger—he indeed should go forth even from the body to enter the blissful state of one who delights in the Self.

Desire first arises in the intellect; here, it directs the mind toward a multitude of objects, and through the senses, it grasps them. From the failure to obtain them, anger manifests. Upon obtaining an object, the intent to preserve it arises as greed. These three constitute the cause of downfall for all; therefore, the wise should abandon them here through the practice of spiritual yoga. 18.

The gift that is performed here by men as an offering to Brahman is [the opposite of] what is known as patience and anger, as well as faith, belief, truth, and goodness—this quartet is called the "bridge" according to the supreme view.

That [bridge] leads to the bondage of living beings; therefore, having crossed over these four by means of the four beginning with generosity, a man attains in this world prosperity, immortality, the heavenly state, and the attainment of light.
Food offered to the gods and guests is nectar; otherwise, food intended solely for oneself is in vain. Indeed, it has been declared here that such food is the very form of death for him.

In this world, he who eats alone becomes a vessel of pure sin among embodied beings. Even that mortal who eats daily according to rule, yet having abandoned the *prāṇāgnihotra* (the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths), is likewise [guilty].

In this world, he alone is a true host who bestows food upon a weary seeker who has come to his home; for him, that food becomes abundant, and he becomes one whose enemies are unborn in the performance of sacrifice.
He who does not give food to a friend seeking it is no friend at all; like a miser who turns away from a constant and devoted servant, such a person desires only his own retreat.
The rise and dissolution of the world, caused respectively by one's own ignorance and knowledge, are common to all living beings from the gods down to those born of earth; so declare the Vedas.

Upon the awakening of the Self, the universe is sublated within Brahman; conversely, upon ignorance, this Brahman is sublated within the world—just as silver is sublated in mother-of-pearl, or as mother-of-pearl is sublated in silver due to mutual delusion. // 22 //

Because of its insubstantiality, there was no "non-existent" (asat), like a flower in the sky; nor was there any "existent" (sat) that could differentiate it. Rather, something other than these two existed then—a state of worldly activity that had not yet reached its cessation.

But what else could it be? It was not the Virāj, preceded by the ether (vyoman), as if it were silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell; rather, in the auspicious Self, it was merely a covering, like the deceptive waters of a mirage.
If bondage consists of the cessation of birth, then liberation likewise did not exist; for just as there is neither night nor day when the sun does not shine, this is merely an optical illusion.

Then, that which was breathless, pure, and one came into being; subsequently, through its own *māyā*, it became known as the "agent. There was nothing else besides it, yet that very same entity became the individual soul (*jīva*), enveloped by the Unborn.

In the beginning, darkness existed in the form of being; therefore, it was hidden by obscurity and inconceivable. Just as water exists within milk, so here is the origin of this world consisting of name and form. From the Creator who desires to emit [the world], the world follows through its own actions; then, by means of the seeds in the form of minds—which first followed and were continuously produced—the effect is brought forth.

She has four braided locks; she may be a young woman, ever-new, or perhaps this eternal Māyā, for she possesses the skill of bringing about the impossible. At the beginning of creation, her face is smeared with ghee as she conceals the very insights of the Vedas. Within her, these two Supreme Persons abide like two birds, through the perception of their respective purposes. (26)
Therein exists one who is unattached; thereafter, another has entered the ocean of ignorance, and having forgotten his own true nature, he beheld a manifestation in the form of the manifold world.

As long as he gazes within with the intellect, the Unborn (Ajā) emits that [world], and she too likewise emits him. Thus, O Brahmins, they who are but one imagine that single One in many ways through their own words.

The inner self does not come at the time of birth, nor does it depart at the time of death; for it is indivisible. It is the *liṅga* (subtle) mind that enters this body or departs from it—upward or downward.

That [self] does not undergo emaciation or bulkiness of the physical form; rather, having taken up the subtle elements (*tejomātrā*) born of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it goes forth, and returns here again together with those very same impressions.
Formerly, there was a priest named Subandhu who served as the chaplain to King Sanātan; having met his death through a lethal spell cast by a rival Brahmin, his mind indeed went to the God of Death.

His brother, however, brought it back again with Vedic mantras, as the Veda declares in a hymn: "Therefore, the mind of one devoted to the Self surely goes [to the Supreme], for the Inner Soul never departs. (29)
The one unshakable Self moves along with the mind as it runs about; yet, though standing before it and behind it, the eyes and other senses do not perceive that which has followed them.
Just as water moves with waves running all around it, so too does the Self exist within them—both before and after—just as it is when those waves, stirred by the wind, have subsided.
Formerly, he was alone, searching for sense-objects in succession within his inner self: "May I have a wife, or offspring, or wealth as an instrument for performing work for that purpose.

Through hardships until his life-breath remains as a mere remnant, he considers nothing else to be more important than this; yet, even upon obtaining one of these, being incomplete, he desists as if dead; and by the loss of even one, feeling his purpose unfulfilled, he grieves.
This cloud, which obscures the sun, did not exist previously, nor does it exist afterwards; rather, while visible, it obstructs the vision of the observer but not the solar disc itself.
If this were not so, then why would the mass of clouds shine without the sun? Like that [cloud], the universe likewise obstructs the vision, yet it does not obstruct its own illuminator and mover.

One who, having enjoyed a kingdom in a dream with all its wealth, upon waking finds himself once again deprived of his kingdom, does not experience such distress, considering that state to be false. Likewise, if one were to commit a sin such as approaching a forbidden woman while dreaming and thereby incur no transgression, one should likewise forget all worldly activity in the waking state as being like a dream.

Whatever auspicious or inauspicious thing is experienced during the state of dream is false upon waking; whatever pertains to the activities of the gross body during the waking state is false at the time of sleep.
Thus, when falsehood is established in both ways, the deluded person remains perpetually attached to it. As for that which makes this [world] appear as real, we truly do not know how it is so here.
Seeing a kinsman alive and awake here, or seeing him dead at the time of sleep, one suddenly feels world-weariness; yet, seeing that same person who was dead as if immortal, one experiences joy.

Even by remembering the death and the departure of breath of this living being, one speaks with him as if he were present; thus, while things appear real, their reality or falsity depends on the power of a brief duration of time.

Just as the emission of semen occurs even from the intense pleasure of union with a woman in a dream—though she is non-existent—so too does this world appear, though it has no real cause and is merely like a reality.

In a dream, the man is real while the young woman here is false, and their union is likewise false; since one finds the soiled garment in the morning, this entire experience is rooted in mental construction.
Every day these living beings see its garden; yet at the time of sleep, no one sees it—this one sporting through illusion apart from the collection of sense organs.

Furthermore, while awake, it is the illuminator and the mover of the multitude of objects and of embodied beings; yet in deep sleep, no one knows it as consisting of supreme bliss. This is truly a marvel! (37)
Instruction in mantras heard in a dream becomes true upon awakening; through the grace of that very dream-state, the desired fruit attains reality in the morning.

Thus, the attainment of truth can indeed arise even from what is unreal. Furthermore, that which is self-luminous is that by which this entire collection of visible phenomena—whether moving or stationary, high or low—shines forth.

In deep sleep, these [deities] such as Fire and Sun, as well as Speech and the others, enter the central vital breath (madhyaprāṇa) which is their own source; thus, the exhaustion mentioned here belongs to them and not to the wind.

The appearance of objects as distinct from them is known to be an illusion, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Therefore, the vow of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is intended in the Upanishads for the attainment of one's own Self, and nothing else.

Fire does not suddenly touch wet fuel; rather, it touches dry fuel during the summer heat. Likewise, even a mind that has been made virtuous through its own performed actions for the sake of progeny and wealth, the fire of knowledge does not touch it all at once, but only when it has been dried by dispassion (*vairāgya*). Therefore, pure dispassion was stated first, and by means of that, the attainment of wisdom (*vijñāna*) is achieved.

Whatever consists of name and form appears here as non-existent, yet it arises on earth by which the world conducts its affairs in manifold ways; that [world] must be concealed by that Lord, just as this double-tongued serpent is restrained by a hidden girdle. When that [Lord] has been abandoned, one enjoys unsurpassed happiness; therefore, do not covet other things such as wealth.

For one desiring liberation, there is first liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and thereafter absolute liberation; these two are obtained through the yoga of practice and knowledge, by means of contact with the compassionate glance of the Guru’s feet. Practice also becomes twofold according to its locus: physical and mental. The physical consists of postures and so forth, while the other is the yoga of knowledge previously described, which is the cessation [of mental activity]. || 42 ||
Having uprooted all desires that have made their abode in the heart—like stakes driven deep—the one who has cast off the conceit of the body and fixed his attention upon the Self abandons fickleness.
Bearing the weight of his accumulated merit, he ascends to the high station through the various channels—blue, white, and ruddy—receiving the bliss of the Self as they pour forth a flood of nectar.
This person here beheld the universe as the Self, transcending sorrow, delusion, and the like; he attained the pure Brahman, for he is indeed the knower of all and the locus of all perfections.
Having forgotten his bodies, gross and subtle, and being devoid of all mental constructs, he—liberated while living—is freed from both merit and sin and has reached the fourth state (turiya).
That vital breath (prāṇa), which reflects the form of the sentient being even when enveloped by the body alone, has manifested unimpaired by the qualities of childhood such as infancy and so forth.
Those of most skillful intellect, possessing the power of true resolve and seeking the divine through practice, lead this superior object of attainment upward along with their matured minds.

Generally, one who has no desire, whose desires have ceased, and who desires only the unsurpassed bliss of the Self, becomes one whose desires are fulfilled upon attaining that [bliss] while abiding in the final stage; at the conclusion of his body, his vital breaths do not depart at all, having reached their sequential cessation within their own respective causes. At that time, where does this living soul dissolve? Like salt in water, it subsequently becomes the indivisible Self alone.
When the water of the ocean becomes solidified within, it is called "saindhava" (rock salt); when thrown back into that same water, it again reaches dissolution and abandons its name and form.

In the same way, the wise man attains dissolution into the Supreme Self; his mind dissolves into the moon, his speech into fire, his eye into the sun, his blood and semen into water, and his ears into the quarters of space.

Just as clarified butter within milk remains unperceived by its sweetness while it exists separately from it, so too does Brahman exist within all beings, known through worldly activity as the seed of rest for the weary.

Know that to be the nectar wherein one finds such gain that all other gains are regarded as mere straw, where no fear arises, and which throbs within as intense bliss; for everything else is indeed afflicted.
Just as a cloth of variegated colors, woven lengthwise and crosswise upon its threads, appears diverse when examined, yet remains nothing but thread;

so too this manifold universe—consisting of mountains, cities, men, villages, animals, and the like—is woven crosswise upon the form of Vairāja, and that [Vairāja] is likewise woven lengthwise and crosswise within Brahman.
Form after form, by virtue of reflection, attains its corresponding likeness; for while there is but one seer, he becomes a second in the water, appearing everywhere in infinite forms.

The Śruti declares that Indra dwells through his powers of illusion (māyā); therefore, the all-pervading Brahman suddenly assumes the state of a living soul (jīvatva) when reflected in the extremely pure limiting adjunct of the intellect (buddhyupādhi).

Those who know that [reality] perceive with their intellect the Supreme Being, endowed with supreme power, as the Creator (Brahmā) reflected within the ocean of consciousness—a locus of rays like a sun—just as the limiting adjunct (upādhi), in whatever form and to whatever extent it exists, reflects the Brahman therein; just as a reflection appears in accordance with the mirror it has reached, so does the Reality always reflect exactly as it is.
Just as the single sun situated there appears manifold within various waters through the power of reflection, and likewise assumes the diversity of the conditions' locations and movements;
so too does the Supreme Self appear as if reflected within high and low beings, seemingly limited by their natures. But in truth, it shines forth clearly, unimpaired by those natures.
Just as the dense nocturnal darkness in a house is utterly destroyed by the rays of the moon reflected in the sun’s rays, or by those concentrated in a bronze vessel;

even so, by the splendors of the Supreme Self being reflected instantaneously within the intellect, objects such as form and the rest shine forth incessantly from all sides through the channels of the sense-organs.

Due to the distinction between the Full Self and the non-Self, that which is here [the Full] is threefold; the other, limited by the intellect (*buddhi*), is likewise threefold, appearing therein like the sky reflected in water. That which is limited by the waters is reflected within this [intellect], both internally and externally. Thus, through the union with the Full and the Limited, ignorance (*avidyā*) dissolves along with its own effects.
Just as countless formidable women are seen simultaneously employed by means of pillars and strings, performing music and all other worldly activities;

so too, because it has entered everywhere and because its power is ever-new and follows all purposes, the world—from Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and Mahas—conducts itself through that which is called the "thread-self" (sūtrātman).

That which is unimpaired throughout the three periods of time—namely, the vital breath, the directions, space, and so forth—in which all this rests, is here declared to be Brahman, the Truth of truths.

There is nothing else whatsoever that is higher or more supreme than this, called the Truth of truths; for while "Being" (sat) and "Non-being" (tyat) constitute the lower truth as conditioned by form and the like, this [Brahman] is the Truth even of that.

Whatever appears as unreal within the sphere of empirical transaction—such as silver, a snake, or water—is indeed dependent upon a substrate of reality; this is the rule established in the world with its limits.

That very reality, which is the Truth of truths, is Brahman, in whom this entire universe has manifested. It is indeed false yet perceived, and for that reason they call it "unreal," while calling Him "Truth. (57)
Where space finds its scope and where time measures but a mere fraction, where indeed the end of hope resides—that Great Virāṭ stands here as if ancient yet as if recent.
Therein the Sūtra appeared, greater even than the Great; for from the Full comes the Full, just as the water of the single ocean arises from the fullness of the oceans and all else.

Just as a single mass of water, through its internal contact with all medicinal herbs, transforms according to their diverse tastes, fragrances, potencies, and post-digestive effects, so too does the Inner Self;
by whose various inherent natures the earth sustains the universe, by whom the cloud rains down profusely, and by whom the fire digests or consumes everything, He is the one who dwells within all.

One should perceive the Self within all beings and the entire multitude of beings as following within the Self, generally like the relationship between water and its waves; then, for a long time, one should see everything as the Self alone.
The non-dual Brahman is the view held in the crest of the Vedas; there is no diversity here at all. He who perceives this world as if it were diverse meets death after death in this world. (60)
Even though there is the cognition that "this space exists before and behind the jar," [the space] appears to arise when the jar arises and perish when it has gone to destruction;

when the jar is moved to another place, [the space] seems to go along with it or to conform to its dimensions—thus does this false perception manifest to embodied beings. In the same way, the Self [is perceived].
As great as the mass of molasses may be, it is nothing but sweetness throughout; as great as a lump of camphor may be, it always transforms here into fragrance alone.

To whatever extent the universe shines forth, delightful with its trees, mountains, cities, gardens, and shrines, to that same extent the one Consciousness expands, since in the end, everything remains as that Self alone.

Even that experience of the sound of a musical instrument is surely dependent upon its striking; there is no separate perception of the sounds of the instrument and the striking, but rather they appear together.

Just as this world, which has Māyā as its material cause, appears as if associated with Brahman, so too, when that [Brahman] is directly perceived, nothing else attains the status of being an object, because [it is sublated by that realization]. || 63 ||
Now, indeed, the Lord of the worlds has been seen directly here; the single, immovable Sthāṇu, the Self of consciousness, has been realized as the inner Self of all beings, pervasive like the sky.

This entire world, apart from Brahman, has been seen to be of the nature of unreality, a mere appearance. "I am the pure Brahman"—with this realization, one should now remain right here, incessantly, free from desire.

When Indra and Indrāṇī enjoy the pleasure of amorous union to their heart's content, there occurs a deep sleep at the end of their dalliance; within that state is a most profound station, dense with bliss, which is the "sheath of bliss" (ānandakośa).

Immersed within that unsurpassed happiness, he knows nothing at all. Thinking, "If he were awakened while in this state, he would become miserable," one of refined intellect should never awaken a sleeping person.

All living beings rejoice when one who has attained fame takes hold of their eyes and other senses, providing them with benefit both internally and externally; they remain in the same state even as in deep sleep.

However, he who dwells in external activity for the sake of filling his belly, being touched by the stains of sin, falls under the power of skin, eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, and thus succumbs to grief and delusion.

While awake, the inner self, exerting manifold efforts for the sake of sensual pleasure, becomes exhausted as the multitude of its senses fatigues; it then falls asleep, forgetting even the pleasure it had attained.

For the sake of rest in one's true nature, however, there arises a bliss that is exceedingly easy to obtain, transcendent of the senses, and supreme—superior indeed to the pleasure born of the senses, which is bitter in its ultimate consequence.
By flapping its wings, the bird generates wind, and by that it rises to a high place; having caught a great current of air, it spreads its own wings and dispels its fatigue.
Alas, this mind, tormented by evil intentions and doubts regarding sense objects, becomes exhausted; for the sake of rest, it sleeps for a long time, stretching out its hands and feet.

Embracing himself, the Self suddenly perceives no distinction whatsoever between the internal and the external, just as a lover who has returned home from a foreign land feels upon tightly embracing his beloved.
Therein, all worldly activity comes to an end; the connection with merit and sin, grief, delusion, or fear—all this, whether even or uneven, he does not remember at all.

The cessation of manifold mental proliferations, whether slight or abundant, the stilling of the senses, and the attainment of bliss—these three are equal in both liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*); however, there is a distinction between them.

One who was asleep due to prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) undergoes awakening and returns once more; but he who is liberated, having destroyed the collection of latent impressions, indeed does not return again. (70)
The king experiences all other joys while enriched with every prosperity; that joy of his, when multiplied a hundredfold, is indeed declared to be the joy of the ancestors (*pitṛs*).

From the world of the gods up to the world of Brahmā, those joys increase by a hundredfold at each stage until they are contained within the single joy of Brahmā; thus, the pleasures derived from sense objects are but a mere fraction of it. (71)

Where bliss (*ānanda*), joy (*moda*), delight (*pramuda*), and rapture (*muda*) abide—all these being attained where all desires cease—therein, in that state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*) resulting from the cessation of everything, make me dwell for a long time in the density of bliss. "Grant to Indra a stream filled with the nectar of the moon," so say the words of the Vedas directed toward Him who is between the two eyebrows. 72.
The unshakable Self, whose nature is bliss, shines forth; yet that which is other than It shines forth otherwise. Thus, stability or instability undergoes transformation within the mind.

Alas, this flickering of the mind is the cause of suffering; for as long as there is the attainment of desired objects, so long will there be in the mind a pleasure born of sense-objects, provided it remains steady. (73)

Just as there is a momentary happiness at the end of sexual union when the mind is one-pointed in its aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and just as there is unsurpassed bliss in deep sleep for as long as it lasts, so too is there eternal bliss in liberation when the heart is stilled. Therefore, since there is a concomitance between happiness and stability here [in these examples], it is appropriate to describe this sensual pleasure as a mere fraction (*mātrā*) of that eternal bliss.

His mind, exhausted by external activities, withdrew from all those [objects] along with their respective latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), for he desired the cessation of that very source [of suffering].

Abandoning within himself the dream-objects produced by the collection of latent impressions—which had been experienced in the dream-body—this [mind] became inclined toward the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) and attained abundant rest therein. (75)

If it is argued that the experience of pleasure and so forth occurs in a dream because a new dream-body—capable of performing those activities—is produced while the [physical] means [of enjoyment] are in a state of stupor, then how can this be? For there is an absence of the necessary causal conditions for such a body. If you say that the dream-body is created by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), then why is the emission of semen not seen when the body falls at the end of sexual intercourse during a dream? (76)
Out of fear it weeps; by this [mind] it speaks, laughs, and boasts; surely, even in a dream, the inner self does not suddenly abandon its attachment to the body, even when one has fainted.

It creates again those very objects previously experienced—the body, the young woman, the horse, the tiger, the country, and so forth—relying upon that body of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-deha*) which consists of the nature of those impressions.

At the junction between waking and deep sleep, there exists a second state known through experience as the dream state; therein the Person (Puruṣa) abides as the light of the Self, having withdrawn all the senses.

Having drawn back the gross body and settled it upon a suitable bed, the Inner Self, by its own radiance, beholds objects of desire in the form of latent impressions and wanders somewhere or other—just like that [the sun].

Protecting with his own life the nest situated at his own bed—remaining there with only his breath as a remnant lest it take on the appearance of a corpse and be devoured by dogs and other scavengers—he creates, through his own power in a dream, horses and chariots, ponds in which he is submerged, numerous places for play, and even imitations of his friends, women, children, and companions. (79)
In one place he sits playing with his beloveds amidst elephants, tigers, bandits, enemies, serpents, and monkeys; in another he laughs or wanders about; and in some places he eats well-prepared food.

In another place he remains suspicious of his own people, thinking, "I have become a barbarian"; in some places he flees out of fear of tigers and other beasts; and in others he weeps while being swallowed [by them]. (80)

Whatever object comes within the range of vision, that very thing flashes forth at that time as it arises from the non-cognition of its own true nature; is this not so, just as the appearance of silver, caused by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, flashes forth as a mere falsehood? And from the cognition of rays of light, water appears, and from the non-cognition of a rope, a serpent appears—causing fear or joy in an instant; therefore, indeed, all this is "creation upon sight" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*).

Since everything has been expanded by me through the locus of the superimposition of Māyā, these [elements] abide in me, yet I do not abide in them; for although silver appears in mother-of-pearl, it does not exist in the silver.
Therefore, the Teacher of All declared that even the elements do not dwell in me, and thus this entire collection of visible objects is indeed false, comparable to a magical illusion.

In this world, action alone is the cause of both happiness and its opposite; thus, the ignorant man, failing to understand this, deals falsely with friends and enemies. Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga spoke thus, and in the palace of King Janaka they likewise praised that very [view] of action. "No one remains here who is devoid of action," so says the crest-jewel of the Yadu lineage. (83)

Although the axe is the instrument for cutting down a tree, it is nevertheless the living being who wields it; likewise, while food is generally the cause of satisfaction, it is declared that the effort of the eater is the actual cause.

Similarly, although past karma is the cause for obtaining fruits that are either unequal or equal, true independence does not indeed belong to this perishable body; rather, its inner self is the true impeller.

Through mindfulness, all actions—whether obligatory or optional, as prescribed for the various castes and stages of life in this world—become an offering unto Brahman; thus the words of the Vedas proclaim most beautifully.
For just as a person is satisfied by gratifying the limbs of the body—the nose, eyes, tongue, hands, feet, head, and ears—so too is the entire tree satisfied by the gratification of its root.

For one who proceeds without knowing the Self—even if he is learned in the scriptures and likewise performs ritual acts—there will be the destruction of that karma after yielding only a meager enjoyment; then, upon returning to rebirth, there is the experience of great suffering.

But for one who knows the Self, even if he desires [worldly fruits], there occurs a great and eternal enjoyment of perfection, for the Self is indeed that perfection; therefore, the Self must certainly be worshipped by one who does not desire any other happiness once it has been attained.

The manifestation of objects does not occur through the sun and other luminaries alone; nor is there anything surprising here in that the sun is not perceived from the sun, nor the moon from the moon, nor fire from fire. Rather, the sun and so forth flash forth when impelled by the consciousness of the eye. Therefore, this person here is his own light; and it is a marvel that he is the great deity of all the gods. (87)

By means of *prāṇa*, he drinks water again and eats food; therein, the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), its strength supported by that [food], performs its digestion quickly or slowly. Then, *vyāna* leads the essence (*rasa*) into all the channels of the limbs for the purpose of nourishing *prāṇa*; and this [wind] known as *apāna* casts out the waste matter, foul-smelling, from the body.

Abiding within the body, this vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of the fivefold functions, is undisputedly the sovereign of all the senses through its constant presence in every form. He who clearly manifests in this manner as the mass of consciousness is I, the witness of all; I am the life of this very breath, and the eye of the eye for all embodied beings. (89)

That which shines as the singular mass of consciousness—the earth, water, wind, sun, moon, and so forth, shine only by following its light, having their own movements thinned away, and they abide within it.

Could even a mass of lightning, a collection of fires, or the vast expanse of the host of stars illuminate that Supreme Lord? For He is the Light, peaceful, infinite, the Seer, unborn, immortal, eternal, and devoid of birth.

If, by the peerless nectar-like glance of the compassionate Śrī Sadguru, the realization "I am indeed that Brahman" arises in any person whatsoever, he alone is liberated while living; with a mind freed from delusion and all doubt dispelled, he enters the supreme abode of eternal bliss once his beginningless limiting adjuncts have vanished. (91)
I am neither the body nor the senses, nor the extremely fickle and decaying mind, nor the intellect, nor the vital breath; "I am not" this entire collection of insentient objects.

I am not egoism, nor wife, house, children, friends, fields, wealth, and so forth—these are far removed from me. I am the witness, the inner conscious Self, the substratum of the entire universe; I am Śiva.

This visible form which appears clearly as many things such as blue, yellow, and so forth, is for everyone the very vision itself; and the eye is the locus of that throbbing experience. That visible object is mental, and even the fluctuations of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*) which take the form of objects through the transformation of vision are themselves visible. In this world, the Lord is of the nature of vision alone; thus He is seen, yet the Witness is not seen at all.

Just as a snake suddenly appears upon a rope in dim darkness due to ignorance of the rope, so too did this state of being a living soul (jīva) become a source of intense suffering for me through ignorance of my own Self.

But when the delusion of the snake ended through the words of a trustworthy person, that single rope was indeed recognized; likewise, by the word of my own Guru, I am the immutable one, not a jīva at all, but Śiva, the witness.

"What is your light? Tell me: during the day it is the sun; at night there are the moon, lamps, and so forth. When the sun, lamps, and such are absent, what light do you have? When the eyes are closed, what happens? There is certainly the intellect (*dhī*). What is the illuminator of that intellect? It is You Yourself. Therefore, O Lord, You are that supreme light, and I am that very light. (95)

Having remained for some time in that state, he no longer assumes a collection of body and so forth here; rather, until the exhaustion of his *prārabdha* karma, he somehow moves about happily with a mind free from attachment.

Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally pure, with the notions of "mine" and "I" dissolved, ever-satisfied, having the nature of the bliss of Brahman, steady-minded, immovable, and with all delusion departed—(96).

That pure, incomparable wisdom which, arising in the intellect of a person, instantly shatters the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman—by that alone is Māyā, the cause of worldly existence, brought to its end; once destroyed, she who fashions the body will never again arise from mere consciousness.

Through the means of valid knowledge that "the universe is not [real]," he abandons the appearance of the world-form which has dissolved away; just as one who has drunk the juice of a fruit utterly discards the fruit itself, though it be rich in fragrance.

Having fully tasted the mouthful of the singular nectar of bliss—the solid mass of Being-Consciousness—within his heart, this self-luminous one, with a tranquil mind, realizes that this entire world is indeed essence-less. (98)

Indeed, his karmas are exhausted, the knot of the heart is rent asunder, and those doubts which yield the fruits of birth and death are utterly severed upon merely beholding the Supreme Lord—He who is of the nature of pure consciousness, free from the impurities of the qualities (*guṇa*), characterized by such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the immutable inner self, the Brahman and the Lord who transcends the scope of all ritual injunctions and the mind. (99)

Having understood that this vast tree of worldly existence— rooted in karma, yielding the fruits of birth and death at its beginning, middle, and end, with delusion, intoxication, joy, and sorrow as its many leaves,

desire and anger as its branches, and sons, cattle, wife, and daughters as its flocks of birds— is to be cut down by the sword of non-attachment, one of keen intellect should contemplate Vāsudeva on all sides.
The entire universe was born from me alone, and once again it is established within me; the whole world dissolves back into me alone—such am I, that very Brahman.

And I bow with great joy to that Acyuta, by the remembrance of whom every ritual action, such as sacrifice and other auspicious rites, reaches perfection even when it has fallen short in this world. 101.

Thus ends the *Śataślokī*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
